FloppyData is the far cheaper option: $10 for 10 GB against $80 at Bright Data's list price, the same flat rate at every volume, and a free cloud anti-detect browser for account work. Bright Data is the better choice for hard targets, enterprise pipelines, precise geo work and compliance-sensitive buyers, where its pool depth, deep targeting, Web Unlocker, SERP API and mature KYC processes justify the cost. Use FloppyData for experiments and easy pages; use Bright Data where failure is expensive.

Bright Data and FloppyData sit at opposite ends of the residential proxy market. Bright Data is the enterprise web-data platform with a 150M+ pool, ZIP, ASN and carrier targeting and managed unblocking products. FloppyData is a young budget provider charging a flat $1/GB on one balance for residential, mobile and datacenter traffic. The price difference at small volumes is eightfold, so this comparison focuses on which jobs need Bright Data and which can run on FloppyData.

blocks.text: Bright Data in 2026: what you get

Bright Data, formerly Luminati, is the default enterprise pick for teams that want every collection tool under one contract. Its residential pool is one of the deepest available (150M+ advertised IPs across 195 countries), targeting goes down to city, ZIP and ASN, and the company layers managed products such as Web Unlocker and the Scraping Browser on top. You pay for that breadth: entry pricing is the highest of the major providers unless a promotion is running, and access to some target categories requires a compliance review.

Strengths: Deepest targeting in the market (ZIP, ASN, carrier); Managed unblocking, SERP and browser products under one account; Mature compliance and KYC processes that enterprise buyers ask for; Very large residential pool for high-rotation work. Weak spots: Highest list price per GB at low volume; Dashboard and zone setup take time to learn; Some targets need a compliance review before access.
FloppyData in 2026: what you get

FloppyData sells proxies the way prepaid phone plans sell minutes: one flat $1/GB balance that works across residential, mobile and datacenter pools. Static residential IPs start at $1.79 each in monthly bundles (20 for $49) with unlimited bandwidth. It is one of the cheapest ways into residential traffic, but it is a newer brand with less independent benchmarking than the established names.

Strengths: Flat $1/GB on any volume; One balance across residential, mobile and datacenter; Cheap static residential bundles with unlimited bandwidth; Free cloud anti-detect browser. Weak spots: Newer brand with limited independent testing; Pool-size claims disputed by some reviewers; Mixed customer-support reviews.
Pricing: Bright Data vs FloppyData

Bright Data lists residential traffic at $8/GB pay-as-you-go with no commitment, and it frequently runs 50%-off promotions that bring that to about $4/GB. Monthly plans start with the Growth tier at $499 for roughly 141 GB (about $3.50/GB) and fall to around $2.50/GB on the largest public plan.

FloppyData charges a flat $1/GB for rotating traffic, and the same balance works for residential, mobile and datacenter IPs. Static residential proxies are sold in monthly bundles from $1.79 per IP (20 IPs for $49), and static datacenter IPs from $0.79 per IP.

At 10 GB a month, FloppyData is the cheaper option at about $10 against $80 for Bright Data, roughly 88% less. Buying 100 GB, you would pay about $100 with FloppyData and $499 with Bright Data: a 80% saving in FloppyData's favour. Both Bright Data and FloppyData work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

FloppyData does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. Bright Data lists '150M+' and FloppyData lists '65M+ claimed (disputed)'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, Bright Data lists 195 countries and FloppyData lists 148 (residential). On targeting, Bright Data offers country, state, city, ZIP, ASN and carrier, while FloppyData offers country and city.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, Bright Data offers rotating per request or sticky sessions you control per zone, and FloppyData offers rotating or sticky sessions. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: Bright Data wins. The deciding factor for Bright Data: its pool depth and Web Unlocker handle hardened targets. The limitation on the FloppyData side: cheap, but with limited independent benchmarking.
SERP and rank tracking: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: it sells a dedicated SERP API alongside raw proxies. How FloppyData compares: workable for light tasks.

Social media and multi-account management: FloppyData wins. The deciding factor for FloppyData: cheap static residential IPs and a free anti-detect browser. The limitation on the Bright Data side: it is powerful but expensive for low-volume account work.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Bright Data wins. The deciding factor for Bright Data: ZIP-level targeting suits local pricing and stock checks. The limitation on the FloppyData side: city targeting at a flat rate.

Ad verification and geo-testing: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: carrier and ASN targeting reproduce what real users see. How FloppyData compares: limited targeting depth and published data.
Tight budgets: FloppyData. FloppyData has the edge here. Why: a flat $1/GB on any volume. How Bright Data compares: its list price is the highest in this comparison.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Bright Data: Free trial for business accounts, no card required. FloppyData: No free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations. Verification and payment rules differ too. Bright Data: Verification required for some sensitive targets. FloppyData: Light. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Bright Data and FloppyData before you commit
The quickest way to choose between Bright Data and FloppyData is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Bright Data: free trial for business accounts, no card required; FloppyData: no free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Bright Data comes out ahead in 4, FloppyData in 2, and 0 are ties. That makes Bright Data the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Bright Data is strongest for enterprise data teams with budget for managed tooling, while FloppyData is strongest for small budgets and experiments. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
